greek: [580] Εἰς τὸ προσηκόντως ἐπὶ τῶν ὀξέως νοσούντων καταστήσασθαι τὴν δίαιταν, ὡς ἐδίδαξε, προστιθέναι κελεύει τήν τε τῆς ἰσχύος ἐπίσκεψιν καὶ τοῦ νοσήματος τὸν τρόπον, ἔτι δὲ τὴν φύσιν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ τὸ ἔθος αὐτοῦ. τὸ μὲν γὰρ κεφάλαιόν ἐστιν, ὃ κατασκευάζει μὴ μεταβάλλειν τὸ τῆς διαίτης εἶδος, πρὸ τοῦ γενέσθαι σαφῆ τὰ τῆς πέψεως σημεῖα· τοῦτο δὲ ἔσται προγνόντος σου πόσαις ἡμέραις τὸ νόσημα πρὸς τὴν ἀκμὴν ἀφίξεται. δυναμένης δὲ τῆς διαίτης, ἣν ἐξελέγξω, κατὰ τὸ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ τὸ ἧττον ἐξαλλάττεσθαι, διὰ τὸ καὶ τοὺς κάμνοντας ἀλλήλων διαφέρειν κατά τε ῥώμην καὶ ἀῤῥωστίαν τῆς δυνάμεως καὶ τὴν φυσικὴν κρᾶσιν καὶ τὸν τρόπον τοῦ νοσήματος καὶ τὸ προγεγονὸς ἔθος, εἰς ταῦτα ἀποβλέποντά σε τεχνικῶς ὑπάρξει στοχάζεσθαι τοῦ τε μᾶλλον καὶ ἧττον τοῦ τῆς διαίτης εἴδους, εἰ ἐπ᾿ ὀξυμέλιτος ἢ μελικράτου τὸν κάμνοντα χρὴ διαιτᾷν ἢ ὕδατος μόνου διδόναι πιεῖν ἄχρι τῶν τῆς πέψεως γνωρισμάτων, ἢ πτισάνην δοτέον ἢ μόνον τὸν χυλὸν αὐτῆς, εἴτ᾿ οὖν δὶς εἴτε καὶ ἅπαξ τῆς ἡμέρας.
rendering_1: [580] For the purpose of properly establishing the regimen in those who are acutely ill, as he has taught, he bids us add in the examination of the strength and the character of the disease, and further the nature of the human being and his habit. For the chief point, which he establishes, is not to change the form of the regimen before the signs of concoction have become clear; and this will be possible once you have foreknown in how many days the disease will arrive at its acme. But since the regimen, which I shall examine (ἐξελέγξω), is capable of being varied in respect of the more and the less, because the patients too differ from one another in the strength and weakness of the faculty and in natural temperament and in the manner of the disease and in the pre-existing habit, by looking to these things it will be possible for you to aim, in accordance with the art, at the more and the less of the form of the regimen: whether one ought to regulate the regimen of the patient on oxymel or melikraton, or to give water alone to drink until the signs of concoction, or whether ptisan is to be given or only its juice, and whether twice or indeed once a day.
rendering_2: [580] For the proper establishment of the regimen in those who are acutely ill, as he has taught, he bids us add both the consideration of the strength and the manner of the disease, and further the nature of the person and his habit. For the main point, which he establishes, is not to change the form of the regimen before the signs of coction have become clear; and this will be the case once you have foreknown in how many days the disease will arrive at its peak. But since the regimen, which I shall scrutinise, can be varied according to the more and the less, because the patients too differ from one another in the robustness and feebleness of the capacity, in the natural mixture, in the manner of the disease and in the previous habit, it will be possible for you, looking to these things, to conjecture skilfully the more and less of the form of the regimen: whether one ought to regulate the diet of the patient on oxymel or on melicrat, or to give water alone to drink until the recognisable signs of coction; or whether ptisan is to be given, or only its juice; and whether twice, or even once, a day.

greek: βλάπτει δὲ καὶ τὰ δεόμενα δι᾿ οὔρων ἐκκαθαίρεσθαι τὰ σώματα· πασῶν γὰρ τῶν ἐκκρίσεων ἐφεκτικός ἐστιν ὁ αὐστηρὸς [648] οἶνος. ταῦτα περὶ οἴνων ὁ Ἱπποκράτης εἰπὼν εὐθὺς ἐπὶ μελίκρατον μεταβαίνει, τὰ μὲν ἄλλα σχεδὸν ἅπαντα τὰ περὶ τῶν οἴνων δείξας, ἓν δὲ παραλιπὼν ἀνεξέργαστον, ὃ διῆλθον ἐγὼ κατὰ τὸ πάρεργον· ὅτι τοῖς πυρέττουσιν οἶνος ἐπιτηδειότατός ἐστιν ὁ ὑδατώδης. ἔστι δ᾿ οὗτος ὁ λευκὸς μὲν τὴν χρόαν, λεπτὸς δὲ τὴν σύστασιν, ἐπιφανῆ μηδεμίαν ἔχων ποιότητα τῶν τοῖς ἄλλοις οἴνοις ὑπαρχουσῶν, μήτ᾿ αὐστηρότητα, μήτε στρυφνότητα, μήτε γλυκύτητα, μήτε δριμύτητα, μήτ᾿ ὀσμήν· τῷ γὰρ τοιούτῳ καὶ τὰς τοῦ ὕδατος κακίας καὶ τὰς τοῦ οἴνου ἐκπεφευγέναι μόνῳ τῶν πάντων οἴνων ὑπάρχει. γεννῶνται δὲ καθ᾿ ἕκαστον ἔθνος ἔνιοι τοιοῦτοι, κατὰ μὲν τὴν Ἰταλίαν ὁ ἄτονος Σαβῖνος, ὃν καὶ διδόασι τοῖς πυρέττουσιν· ἐν Ἀσίᾳ δὲ ὅ τε Τιτακαζηνὸς καὶ Τιβῖνος.
rendering_1: And it also harms those bodies that need to be purged through the urine; for the austere [648] wine is retentive of all the excretions. Having said these things about wines, Hippocrates passes straight on to melikraton, having set out nearly all the other points concerning wines, but leaving one unworked-out, which I went through as a side matter: that for those with fever the most suitable wine is the watery one. This is the wine white in colour, thin in consistency, having no manifest quality of those that belong to the other wines—neither austerity, nor harshness, nor sweetness, nor pungency, nor odour; for it belongs to such a wine alone of all wines to have escaped both the faults of water and those of wine. Some such wines are produced in each nation: in Italy the slack Sabine, which they also give to those with fever; in Asia the Titacazene and the Tibine.
rendering_2: It also harms those bodies that need to be cleansed out through the urine; for austere [648] wine is retentive of all excretions. Having said these things about wines, Hippocrates passes straight on to honey-water (melikraton). He has set out almost everything else concerning wines, but has left one point unworked out, which I went through by way of a side-issue: that for those who are feverish the most suitable wine is the watery one. This is the wine that is white in colour and thin in consistency, and that has no evident quality of those belonging to the other wines: neither austerity, nor acerbity, nor sweetness, nor pungency, nor smell. For to such a wine alone of all wines it belongs to have escaped both the defects of water and those of wine. Some such wines are produced in each nation: in Italy the weak Sabine, which they also give to the feverish; and in Asia the Titakazene and the Tibine.

greek: ἀλλοιοῦται μὲν οὖν ἀθρόως κατὰ τὰς δραστικὰς [516] ποιότητας θερμαινόμενα καὶ ψυχόμενα καὶ ξηραινόμενα καὶ ὑγραινόμενα, διαφθείρεται δ᾿ αὐτῶν ἡ συνέχεια τεινομένων σφοδρῶς ἢ θλιβομένων. οὕτως οὖν καὶ τῆς πλευρᾶς ὀδύνη γίγνεται κατὰ τὰ πλευριτικὰ πάθη, περὶ ὧν ὁ λόγος ἦν αὐτῷ, τῆς ἐν τούτοις τοῖς χωρίοις φλεγμονῆς καὶ τῷ πλήθει τῆς παρὰ φύσιν θερμασίας ἀνιώσης τὰ μόρια κατὰ δυσκρασίαν καὶ τῇ πληρώσει δὲ τεινούσης τὰ φλεγμαίνοντα σώματα. πρώτης οὖν ἀξιοῖ βοηθείας εἰς τὴν τῆς ὀδύνης ἴασιν ἢ παρηγορίαν ἀποπειραθῆναι τῆς διὰ τῶν θερμασμάτων· ταῦτα γὰρ εἴωθεν ἀραιόν τε τὸ δέρμα πρὸς τὰς διαπνοὰς ἐργάζεσθαι καὶ τὸ κατὰ τὴν φλεγμονὴν αἷμα λεπτύνειν τε καὶ διαφορεῖν. εἰ μὲν οὖν ταῦτα πραχθείη, κενωθήσεταί τι τοῦ αἵματος ἧττόν τε διατεινόμενα τὰ πεπονθότα μόρια πρὸς τοῦ λοιποῦ πρᾳότερον ὀδυνήσεται· μὴ γιγνομένου δὲ ἐλάττονος τοῦ κατὰ τὴν φλεγμονὴν αἵματος ἢ καὶ πνεύματος ἀτμώδους ἐκ τῆς θερμασίας γεννηθέντος αὐξάνεσθαι συμβαίνει τὴν ὀδύνην.
rendering_1: They are altered all at once, then, in respect of the active [516] qualities when they are heated and cooled and dried and moistened, whereas their continuity is destroyed when they are violently stretched or compressed. In this way, then, pain of the side also arises in the pleuritic affections, about which his discussion was concerned, the inflammation in these regions both distressing the parts, by way of dyskrasia, through the abundance of heat contrary to nature, and also, by its filling, stretching the inflamed bodies. He therefore thinks it right that, for the cure or soothing of the pain, trial be made first of the remedy by means of warming applications; for these are accustomed to render the skin rare for transpirations and to thin and disperse the blood that is in the inflammation. If, then, these things are accomplished, some of the blood will be evacuated, and the affected parts, being less distended by what remains, will suffer pain more mildly; but if the blood in the inflammation does not become less, or if also vaporous pneuma is generated from the heat, it comes about that the pain increases.
rendering_2: They are altered all at once, then, in respect of the active [516] qualities, when they are heated, cooled, dried and moistened; and their continuity is destroyed when they are violently stretched or compressed. In this way, then, pain of the side also arises in the pleuritic affections, which were the subject of his discussion: the inflammation in these regions both distresses the parts through dyscrasia, by the abundance of the unnatural heat, and stretches the inflamed bodies by its repletion. He therefore thinks it right, as the first remedy for the cure or the soothing of the pain, to try the one by means of hot applications; for these customarily make the skin porous for transpirations, and thin and disperse the blood in the inflammation. If, then, this should be accomplished, some of the blood will be evacuated, and the affected parts, being less distended, will thereafter suffer pain more mildly; but if the blood in the inflammation does not become less, or if vaporous pneuma has also been generated from the heat, it comes about that the pain increases.

greek: ταύτην μὲν οὖν τὴν ῥῆσιν ἐξηγήσομαι, νυνὶ δὲ ἐπὶ τὴν προκειμένην ἐπανήξω, τήνδε τὴν διάνοιαν ἔχουσαν· [573] οὐχ οἷόν τέ ἐστι παρὰ καιρὸν οὔτε σφόδρα λιμαγχονεῖν οὔτ᾿ ἐν ταῖς ἀκμαῖς τῶν νοσημάτων μεταβάλλειν τὴν δίαιταν ἐξ ἐνδείας ἐπὶ προσφορὰν, ὥσπερ οὐδ᾿ ἐπὶ τοὐναντίον ἀθρόως· οἷς ἕπεται δηλονότι τὸ τοιαύτην ποιεῖσθαι τὴν δίαιταν οἵαν οὗτος ἐκέλευσε· κεφάλαιον δὲ αὐτῆς ἐστι πεφυλάχθαι τὰς ἀθρόας μεταβολὰς ἐπὶ τἀναντία. Πολλὰ δ᾿ ἄν τις ἠδελφισμένα τούτοισι τῶν ἐς κοιλίην καὶ ἄλλα εἴποι· ὡς εὐφόρως μὲν φέρουσι τὰ βρώματα ἃ εἰθισμένοι εἰσὶν, ἢν καὶ μὴ ἀγαθὰ ᾖ φύσει, ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ τὰ ποτά· δυσφόρως δὲ φέρουσι τὰ βρώματα, ἃ μὴ εἰθισμένοι εἰσὶν, ἢν καὶ μὴ κακὰ ᾖ, ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ τὰ ποτά.
rendering_1: This passage, then, I shall expound; but for now I shall return to the one before us, which has the following meaning: [573] it is not possible, contrary to the right occasion, either to starve severely or, at the peaks of diseases, to change the regimen from deficiency to administration of food, just as neither is it possible to change all at once in the opposite direction; from which it clearly follows that one should make the regimen such as he enjoined; and the main point of it is to have guarded against sudden changes to the opposites. One might mention many other things too, akin to these, among those that concern the belly: that people bear easily the foods to which they are accustomed, even if they are not good by nature, and likewise also the drinks; but they bear with difficulty the foods to which they are not accustomed, even if they are not bad, and likewise also the drinks.
rendering_2: This passage, then, I shall explain; but for now I shall return to the one before us, which has the following sense: [573] it is not possible either to subject to starvation unseasonably or severely, or, at the peaks of diseases, to change the regimen from deficiency to administration of food, just as it is not possible to change it suddenly in the opposite direction either. From these it obviously follows that one should adopt a regimen such as he prescribed, and its main point is to guard against sudden changes to the opposite. 'Many other things akin as brothers to these, relating to the belly, one could also mention: how people tolerate easily the foods to which they are accustomed, even if they are not good by nature, and likewise also the drinks; and how they tolerate with difficulty the foods to which they are not accustomed, even if they are not bad, and likewise also the drinks.'

greek: τὰ δὲ κατὰ τὰς ὠμοπλάτας τε καὶ τὸν ἐν τῷ τραχήλῳ νωτιαῖον ἐκ τῶν κάτω μερῶν τῆς εἰρημένης ῥίζης κοινῆς ἔχει τὰς φλέβας ἀνερχομένας ἐπ᾿ αὐτά· λέγω δὲ κοινὴν ῥίζαν ἢν ἀρτίως εἶπον εἶναι [531] ταῖς τε ἐπιπολαίοις σφαγίτισι καὶ ταῖς ὠμιαίαις. εἰκότως οὖν ἡ μὲν ὠμιαία τὰ τῶν κλειδῶν ἄνωθεν μέρη κενοῖ θᾶττόν τε καὶ μᾶλλον, ὅσα κατὰ τράχηλόν τέ ἐστι καὶ κεφαλήν· ἡ δὲ διὰ τῆς μασχάλης τὰ κατὰ τὸν θώρακα καὶ τούτων αὐτῶν μᾶλλον τὰ ὑψηλὰ καὶ μάλιστα ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων· ἐπειδὴ τὰ ταπεινὰ πάντα μία φλὲψ ἑτέρα τρέφει κατωτέρω τῆς καρδίας ἀποφυομένη τῆς κοίλης φλεβός. ταύτης δὲ τῆς τὰ ταπεινὰ τοῦ θώρακος τρεφούσης παρὰ τὰς ῥίζας τῶν πλευρῶν κατάντους φερομένης ἐκ τῶν ἀριστερῶν μερῶν ἄχρι τοῦ διαφράγματος, αἱ καθ᾿ ἕκαστον μεσοπλεύριον, ἀριστερόν τε καὶ δεξιὸν, ἀπονεμήσεις γίγνονται· καὶ μέντοι καὶ τὸ λείψανον αὐτῆς διεκπίπτει πρὸς τὸ διάφραγμα τοῖς πρώτοις μετ᾿ αὐτὸ διανεμόμενον σώμασιν. αἱ δὲ διὰ τῶν μασχαλῶν ἐπὶ τὰς χεῖρας φερόμεναι τὰς ῥίζας ἔχουσιν ἐγγυτάτω ταῖς τρεφούσαις φλεψὶ τὰς ὑψηλὰς τοῦ θώρακος τέτταρας πλευρὰς, οὐκ ὀλίγῳ μείζους οὖσαι τῶν κατὰ τὸν ὦμον εἰς τὰς χεῖρας ἡκουσῶν.
rendering_1: But the parts about the shoulder-blades and the spinal marrow in the neck have the veins that ascend to them from the lower portions of the aforementioned common root; and by common root I mean the one that I just now said belongs [531] to the superficial jugulars and to the humeral veins. Reasonably, then, the humeral vein evacuates more quickly and to a greater degree the parts above the collar-bones, namely all those that lie in the neck and head; whereas the vein that passes through the armpit evacuates the parts in the thorax, and of these themselves more the upper ones, and especially in human beings; since all the lower parts are nourished by one other vein, which branches off from the vena cava lower down than the heart. And from this vein that nourishes the lower parts of the thorax, which runs downward alongside the roots of the ribs on the left side as far as the diaphragm, the distributions into each intercostal space, both left and right, arise; and moreover what remains of it passes out through to the diaphragm, being distributed to the first bodies after it. But the veins that pass through the armpits to the arms have their roots very close to the veins that nourish the four upper ribs of the thorax, being not a little larger than those that come to the arms by way of the shoulder.
rendering_2: The parts at the shoulder blades and the spinal marrow in the neck have their veins, which ascend to them, from the lower parts of the aforementioned common root; by 'common root' I mean the one which I said just now belongs [531] both to the superficial jugular veins and to the humeral veins. It is reasonable, then, that the humeral vein evacuates the parts above the collarbones, namely those in the neck and head, more quickly and to a greater degree, while the vein through the armpit evacuates the parts in the thorax, and of these themselves the upper ones more, and most of all in human beings; since all the lower parts are nourished by another, single vein, which branches off from the vena cava below the heart. As this vein, which nourishes the lower parts of the thorax, is carried downward along the roots of the ribs on the left side as far as the diaphragm, distributions are made to each intercostal space, left and right; and moreover its remainder passes through to the diaphragm, being distributed to the first bodies after it. The veins carried through the armpits to the arms have their roots very close to the veins that nourish the upper four ribs of the thorax, and they are not a little larger than those that come to the arms by way of the shoulder.

greek: εἶτα περὶ τῶν ὑστερικῶν γινομένων, εἶτα περὶ τοῦ μηκωνείου, εἶθ᾿ ἑξῆς ὑδραγωγὸν φάρμακον, εἶτ᾿ ἐκκοπρωτικὸν, εἶθ᾿ ἑδρικοῖς, ὑδερικοῖς τε δίδωσι διὰ μηκωνείου καὶ [919] ἰτρίων. ἔστιν οὖν ἐφεξῆς τῶν εἰρημένων τὰ μὲν πλεῖστα σαφῆ, παρέγκειται δέ τινα καὶ ἀσαφῆ, περὶ ὧν ἐφεξῆς ποιήσομαι τὸν λόγον.
rendering_1: Then about the affections arising from the womb (hysterical affections), then about mekonion, then next a hydragogue drug, then one that expels faeces, then for those with complaints of the seat (anus) and for the dropsical he gives [a remedy] made through mekonion and [919] itria (sesame-cakes). Now, of what follows after the things that have been said, most are clear, but certain obscure things are also inserted, about which I shall make my account in what follows.
rendering_2: Then about what occurs in uterine affections, then about the mēkōnion (poppy juice), then next a hydragogue drug, then an evacuant of faeces, then for patients with complaints of the seat and for dropsical patients he gives a preparation made with mēkōnion and [919] itria (thin cakes). Of what follows the things already said, then, most is clear, but some unclear things have also been inserted alongside, and these I shall discuss next.

greek: ἀσφαλῶς δὲ προσέθηκεν, εἰ μὴ ταράσσει τὴν κοιλίαν, ἐπὶ τοῦ μελικράτου τὸν λόγον ποιούμενος· ἐκείνους γὰρ δεόντως καὶ χείρονας ἑαυτῶν ἐργάζεται διὰ τὴν κένωσιν, οἶς ταράσσει τὴν κοιλίαν· ἅμα καὶ τοῦ [668] ταράττειν ῥήματος οὐ τὴν σύμμετρον ὑποχώρησιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν πλεονάζουσαν δηλοῦντος. εἰδέναι μέντοι χρὴ τὸ μὲν ὠμὸν μελίκρατον ὑπακτικώτερον εἶναι, τὸ δὲ καλῶς ἡψημένον τροφιμώτερον· ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μὲν ἐγνώσθω σοι κατὰ τὸ πάρεργον, ἴδωμεν δὲ ἃ ἑξῆς γράφει παραβάλλων οἴνῳ μελίκρατον. Ἀτὰρ καὶ οἴνου λευκοῦ καὶ λεπτοῦ καὶ ὀλιγοφόρου καὶ ἀνόσμου ᾗ μὲν ἰσχυρότερόν ἐστιν, ᾗ δὲ ἀσθενέστερον. Ἔνιοι χωρὶς τοῦ ἐστὶ γράφουσι τὴν ῥῆσιν οὕτως· ἀτὰρ καὶ οἴνου λεπτοῦ καὶ ὀλιγοφόρου καὶ ἀνόσμου ᾗ μὲν ἰσχυρότερον, ᾗ δὲ ἀσθενέστερον. ἔνιοι δὲ ἀντὶ τοῦ ᾗ τὸ ἐνίῃ γράφουσιν οὕτως· ἀτὰρ καὶ οἴνου ὀλιγοφόρου καὶ λεπτοῦ καὶ ἀνόσμου ἐνίῃ μὲν ἰσχυρότερον, ἐνίῃ δὲ ἀσθενέστερον. ἐξ ἁπάντων γε μὴν ἡ αὐτὴ δηλοῦται δύναμις καὶ ἔννοια, κατά τι μὲν λέγοντος ἰσχυρότερον εἶναι τὸ μελίκρατον τοῦ τοιούτου οἴνου, κατά τι δὲ ἀσθενέστερον.
rendering_1: He added, with good reason, 'if it does not disturb the belly' when he was speaking about melicrat; for in those whose belly it disturbs, it naturally makes them worse than they were, because of the evacuation. At the same time the word 'to disturb' [668] indicates not the moderate discharge but the excessive one. One must know, however, that raw melicrat is more laxative, whereas well-boiled melicrat is more nourishing. But let this be known to you as a side-remark; let us see what he writes next, comparing melicrat with wine. 'Moreover, compared with white, thin, oligophoros (of little bearing) and odourless wine, it is in one respect stronger, in another weaker.' Some people write the phrase without the 'is', thus: 'Moreover, compared with thin, oligophoros and odourless wine, in one respect stronger, in another weaker.' Others write 'in some respects' (eniēi) instead of 'in one respect' (hēi), thus: 'Moreover, compared with oligophoros, thin and odourless wine, in some respects stronger, in some respects weaker.' From all of them, however, the same meaning and sense is made clear: he is saying that melicrat is in some respect stronger than such a wine, and in some respect weaker.
rendering_2: And he safely added "if it does not disturb the belly", making his statement about melikraton; for it rightly makes those persons even worse than they were, by reason of the emptying, in whom it disturbs the belly—at the same time, the word [668] "disturb" indicates not the moderate evacuation but the excessive one. One must know, however, that raw melikraton is more laxative, while that which has been well boiled is more nourishing; but let this be known to you as a side-point, and let us look at what he writes next, comparing melikraton with wine. "But also in relation to wine that is white and thin and bears little water and is odourless, in one respect it is stronger, in another weaker." Some write the passage without the "is", thus: "but also in relation to wine that is thin and bears little water and is odourless, in one respect stronger, in another weaker." Others write ἐνίῃ instead of ᾗ, thus: "but also in relation to wine that bears little water and is thin and odourless, in one respect (ἐνίῃ) stronger, in one respect weaker." From all of them, nonetheless, the same force and meaning is indicated, since he says that melikraton is in some respect stronger than such a wine, and in some respect weaker.

greek: [820] Εἰσὶ δὲ ὄψιες πολλαὶ τῶν καμνόντων. Ὄψιας εἴρηκεν ὡσανεὶ διαφορὰς ἢ τρόπους ἢ ἰδέας· τῶν καμνόντων δὲ, ἀντὶ τοῦ τῶν τοῖς κάμνουσιν γινομένων νοσημάτων. ἐδείχθη γὰρ ἤδη πολλάκις ὡς ἅπασι τοῖς παλαιοῖς ἔθος ἐστὶν ἀπὸ τε τῶν παθημάτων ἐπὶ τοὺς πάσχοντας αὐτοὺς μεταφέρειν τὰς προσηγορίας, ἀπό τε τῶν πασχόντων ἐπὶ τὰ πάθη· ὡς μηδὲν διαφέρειν τῶν πυρετῶν εἰπεῖν διαφορὰς ἢ τῶν πυρεττόντων, οὕτως δὲ καὶ πλευριτικῶν ἢ συναγχικῶν ἢ πλευρίτιδος ἢ συνάγχης. ὄψιας οὖν εἶπε καμνόντων, ἐπειδὴ τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοὺς θεωροῦντες εὑρίσκομεν τὰς διαφοράς. Διὸ προσεκτέον τῷ ἰωμένῳ, ὅκως μὴ διαλήσεταί τις τῶν προφασίων.
rendering_1: [820] There are many appearances of the sick. He has said "appearances" as if to say differences or modes or forms; and "of the sick" in place of "of the diseases that arise in the sick." For it has already been shown many times that it is customary for all the ancients to transfer the appellations both from the affections to the sufferers themselves and from the sufferers to the affections, so that it makes no difference whether one speaks of the differences of fevers or of those who have fever, and likewise of pleuritics or synanchics, or of pleuritis or synanche. So he said "appearances of the sick," since it is by observing them with our eyes that we discover the differences. Therefore the one who treats must pay attention, so that none of the occasioning causes (προφάσιες) escapes his notice.
rendering_2: [820] There are many aspects of the patients. He has called them 'aspects' as if to say differences, or modes, or forms; and 'of the patients' in place of 'of the diseases that occur in the patients'. For it has already been shown many times that it is the custom of all the ancients to transfer designations from the affections to those who are themselves affected, and from those affected to the affections, so that it makes no difference whether one speaks of the differences of fevers or of feverish patients, and likewise of pleuritic patients or synanchic patients, or of pleuritis or synanchē. He therefore said 'aspects of patients', since it is by observing them with our eyes that we find the differences. Therefore the one who heals must pay attention, so that none of the occasions escapes his notice.

greek: οὕτω μὲν ὄξος τὰ νευρώδη μόρια βλάπτει· τὴν μήτραν δ᾿ ἅπαντες σχεδὸν οἱ ἀνατομικοὶ λέγουσιν εἶναι νευρώδη· καὶ χωρὶς δὲ τῆς ἐκείνων ἀποφάσεως, ἣν ἐκ τῆς ἀνατομικῆς αὐτοψίας ἐποιήσαντο, πάρεστί σοι συλλογίσασθαι περὶ αὐτῆς, ὡς ἐπὶ πλεῖστον μὲν διαστελλομένης, εἰς ἐλάχιστον δὲ συνιζανούσης· ἀεὶ γὰρ ὁπηλίκον ἂν εἴη τὸ ἔμβρυον, ἐν κύκλῳ περιείληφεν αὐτὸ καὶ πεπλήρωται τὸ πᾶν κύτος ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνου, κᾂν μικρὸν ᾖ, καθάπερ καὶ ἡ γαστὴρ ὑπὸ τῶν σιτίων· ἀλλὰ ταύτης μὲν οὐ μεγάλη πρὸς τἀναντία ἡ μεταβολὴ, τῆς μήτρας δὲ μέγισται· τὸ δὲ ἐπὶ πλεῖστον [695] διαστέλλεσθαι νευρωδῶν ἴδιόν ἐστι σωμάτων, οὐ σαρκωδῶν. Ὕδατι δὲ ποτῷ ἐν τῇσιν ὀξείῃσι νούσοισιν ἄλλο μὲν οὐδὲν ἔχω ἔργον ὅ τι προσθέω. οὔτε γὰρ βηχὸς παρηγορικόν ἐστιν ἐν τοῖσι πλευριτικοῖσι καὶ περιπνευμονικοῖσιν, οὔτε πτυέλου ἀναγωγὸν, ἀλλ᾿ ἧσσον τῶν ἄλλων εἴ τις διὰ παντὸς ὕδατι ποτῷ χρέοιτο· μεσσηγὺ μέντοι ὀξυμέλιτος καὶ μελικρήτου ὕδωρ ἐπιῤῥοφεόμενον ὀλίγον πτυέλου ἀναγωγόν ἐστι, διὰ τὴν μεταβολὴν τῆς ποιότητος τῶν ποτῶν, πλημμυρίδα γάρ τινα ἐμποιέει ἄλλως δὲ οὐδὲ δίψαν παύει, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπιπικραίνει· χολῶδες γὰρ φύσει χολώδει καὶ ὑποχονδρίῳ κακὸν καὶ κάκιστον ἑωυτοῦ καὶ χολωδέστατον καὶ φιλαδυναμιώτατον, ὅταν ἐς κενότητα ἐσέλθῃ.
rendering_1: In this way, then, vinegar harms the sinewy parts. Nearly all the anatomists say that the uterus is sinewy. Even apart from their pronouncement, which they made from first-hand anatomical observation, you can reason it out about the uterus, since it dilates to the greatest extent and contracts to the smallest. For however large the embryo may be at any time, the uterus always encloses it all round, and its whole cavity is filled by it even when it is small, just as the stomach is filled by foods. But the change of the stomach towards the opposite states is not great, whereas the changes of the uterus are very great. And to be dilated to the greatest extent [695] is peculiar to sinewy bodies, not to fleshy ones. As for water as a drink in acute diseases, I have no other effect of it that I can add. For in pleuritic and peripneumonic cases it neither soothes cough nor brings up sputum, but does so less than the others if one uses water as a drink throughout. Water sipped a little in between oxymel and melicrat, however, brings up sputum because of the change in the quality of the drinks, for it produces a kind of flood-tide. Otherwise it does not even stop thirst, but makes things more bitter. For it is bilious to a bilious nature and bad for the hypochondrium; and it is at its worst, most bilious and most conducive to loss of strength when it enters into emptiness.
rendering_2: Thus vinegar harms the sinewy parts; and nearly all the anatomists say that the womb is sinewy. And even apart from their pronouncement, which they made on the basis of anatomical direct inspection (autopsia), it is open to you to reason about it from the fact that it is dilated to the greatest extent and shrinks together to the least: for always, however large the embryo may be, it encloses it in a circle and its whole cavity is filled by it, even if it is small, just as the stomach also is by foods; but in the case of the stomach the change toward the opposite states is not great, whereas in the case of the womb the changes are very great; and being dilated to the greatest extent [695] is a property peculiar to sinewy bodies, not to fleshy ones. As for water as a drink in acute diseases, I have no other function that I could add. For it is neither soothing of cough in pleuritic and peripneumonic patients, nor does it bring up sputum, but it does so less than the other drinks, if one should use water as drink throughout; however, water sipped in small quantity in between oxymel and melikraton does bring up sputum, because of the change in the quality of the drinks, for it produces a kind of flood-tide; otherwise it does not even stop thirst, but makes it more bitter; for it is bilious for a bilious nature and bad for the hypochondrium, and it is at its own worst and most bilious and most apt to produce weakness (philadynamiōtaton), when it enters into emptiness.

greek: Οἱ μὲν πλεῖστοι τῶν ἐξηγουμένων βέλτιον τοῖς προειρημένοις συντάττουσι ταῦτα, περὶ τῶν θερμὴν ἐχόντων τὴν κάτω κοιλίην ἡγούμενοι καὶ νῦν ἔτι γίγνεσθαι τὸν λόγον· [898] ὀλίγοι δέ τινες ἀποχωρίσαντες ἰδίᾳ ταῦτα ἐξηγοῦνται· σκοπὸς δέ ἐστιν αὐτοῖς τὸ μέν τι καθᾶραι τῆς κακοχυμίας, τὸ δ᾿ ἐπικεράσαι, τὸ δ᾿ ἐπιξηρᾶναι, τὸ δ᾿ ἐμψῦξαι. τὸ μὲν οὖν γάλα τὸ ὄνειον καθαίρειν δύναται καὶ ἐπικεραννύναι, τὸ δὲ τοῦ λίνου σπέρμα ξηραίνειν τε καὶ ψύχειν· τὰ δ᾿ ἐκ τῶν πυρῶν ἄλφιτα τὸ ἐπικεραστικὸν ἔχει· καλῶς δ᾿ αὐτοῖς ἀναμέμικται καὶ τὰ κρίθινα, ξηραίνοντά τε καὶ ψύχοντα. οἱ δὲ Αἰγύπτιοι κύαμοι μετρίως ψῦξαι δύνανται· τὰ δὲ ὠὰ καὶ ἡ σεμίδαλις καὶ ὁ χόνδρος παχύχυμα καὶ εὔχυμα καὶ ἐπικρατητικά· καὶ ξηραίνει δὲ ἱκανῶς ὡς ἐν ἐδέσμασιν ἡ κέγχρος, ὥσπερ γε καὶ ψύχει. ταῦτα δὲ πάντα δίδωσι ψυχρὰ, διὰ τὴν δριμύτητα καὶ θερμότητα τῶν τὸ πάθος ἐργαζομένων χυμῶν.
rendering_1: Most of the commentators, and with better reason, join these words to what was said before, holding that the discussion is even now still about those who have a hot lower belly; [898] but a certain few separate them off and explain them on their own. Their aim is partly to purge away some of the bad humour (kakochymia), partly to temper it, partly to dry it, partly to cool it. Now asses' milk is able to purge and to temper, and the seed of flax to dry and to cool; the groats made from wheat have the tempering property; and barley groats too are fittingly mixed in with them, since they dry and cool. Egyptian beans are able to cool moderately; eggs, fine wheat-meal (semidalis) and groats (chondros) are productive of thick humour and of good humour, and are capable of prevailing (ἐπικρατητικά; the reading is doubtful, perhaps 'tempering'). And millet dries considerably, as foods go, just as it also cools. All these he gives cold, on account of the acridity and heat of the humours that produce the affection.
rendering_2: Most of the commentators, better, connect these words with what has been said before, holding that the discussion is still now concerning those who have a hot lower belly; [898] but a few, separating them off, interpret them on their own. The aim in these prescriptions is partly to purge the bad humours (κακοχυμία), partly to temper, partly to dry up, and partly to cool. Asses' milk, then, is able to purge and to temper, while linseed is able to dry and to cool; the alphita made from wheat possess the tempering quality; and the barley ones too are well mixed in with them, drying and cooling. The Egyptian beans are able to cool moderately; the eggs, the fine wheat flour (σεμίδαλις) and the groats (χόνδρος) are thick-juiced, of good juice, and ἐπικρατητικά (prevailing, overpowering); and millet dries sufficiently, as far as foods go, just as it also cools. All these he gives cold, on account of the acridity and heat of the humours producing the affection.
